diagnostic_evidence.quote:
\item The specular directional derivative $\partial^{\sd}_v f(x)$ exists.
        \item $\partial^+_v f(x)$ and $\partial^-_v f(x)$ exist as extended real numbers, but they cannot be simultaneously $\infty$ or $-\infty$.
diagnostic_evidence.tag: cor: representation with A of the specular directional derivative

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem and corollary claim that existence of the specular derivative is equivalent to existence of both one-sided derivatives. However, the specular derivative is a limit of tan of half the sum of arctans of the two difference quotients. The two quotients can oscillate in a coordinated way so their arctan sum has a limit while neither one-sided derivative exists. For example, set the right quotient to tan(pi/4 + delta sin(1/h)) and the left to tan(pi/4 - delta sin(1/h)); then the arctan sum is constant, so the specular derivative exists, but the one-sided derivatives do not.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof needs sum h_l = infinity to obtain a contradiction, but the assumptions only give sum t_l = infinity and sum t_l^2 < infinity. Since h_l = t_l / ||nabla^s f(x_l)||, the sum of h_l can be finite if the gradient norms are unbounded. No bound on the gradient norms is established at this point.
